name: Marco Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm with Castleton Fit-Out, a commercial firm of about forty electricians, and right now I'm on a shopping centre refit. Half my week is nights, because the shops trade in the day. It's lighting, cable tray, which is the metal channel the cables sit in, distribution boards, then testing at the end. I like the first night all the new lights come on across a whole floor. What wears me down is drawings that are wrong and the drive home at six in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, and I rent a two-bed flat with Leah, my fiancée, who's a dental nurse. We've got about three months of money saved between us. Weekends I fit EV chargers, the car charging points, for neighbours and family, which brings in a bit extra. Fridays I go to the mosque with my dad when the shifts allow.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll ask a chatbot to tidy up the wording on a quote for a weekend job, or to remind me of a cable size before I check it in the regulations book. I don't trust it on its own, I always check the book. The way I see it, it's like a new apprentice, handy but you watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad says about everything new: let's see it work first. At the site canteen I'd tell the lads the whole fuss was a sales pitch. I don't post online, so that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. Commercial work is busy, the shopping centre job runs till next autumn, and my weekend charger jobs add about a fifth to my pay. The only thing that nags is the rent going up again in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep on with the firm and keep doing two or three EV chargers a month on weekends, and put that weekend money aside for the wedding. I'd keep using the chatbot for quote wording, because it saves me half an hour on a Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, really. Life would go to plan, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent going up. How much does that press on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's annoying, not frightening. Leah and I split it, and between my weekend jobs and her shifts at the dental surgery we're managing. If it goes up again, we'd look at a cheaper flat further out, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone at work who's worried anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say look at the job in front of you. Ray, our foreman, has been running sites for thirty years and he's seen every new gadget come and go. A cable tray still has to go up a ladder and get bolted to the ceiling by a person.

say: I'd say let's see it **work first**, like my dad says about everything new.
I'd tell the lads in the **site canteen** the fuss was a sales pitch.
think: Commercial work is **busy** and the shopping centre job runs till next autumn.
Weekend **charger jobs** add about a fifth to his pay.
The only nag is **rent rising** again in spring.
do: Keep working at **Castleton** on the shopping centre refit.
Fit two or three **EV chargers** a month on weekends.
Put the **weekend money** aside for the wedding.
feel: **Calm** and comfortable, with life going roughly to plan.
S0.quote: A cable tray still has to go up a ladder and get bolted to the ceiling by a person.
fieldNote: He borrows his **father's caution**: new things must prove themselves first.
His **side income** from EV chargers gives him a real buffer against rent rises.
He uses a chatbot lightly but **checks the book**, treating AI like an apprentice.

steps.text: Keep working on the shopping centre refit with Castleton
Fit two or three EV chargers a month on weekends
Put all the weekend job money aside for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly the office side's problem, and that the trades are the last thing to go. I'd say it to Leah and to my dad. Online I wouldn't say anything, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've already seen a bit of this. Our firm prices jobs from the drawings with software now, and they didn't replace an estimator who left in the summer. If the planning and ordering go to software, there are fewer supervisor jobs to step up into, and that's where I hoped to be in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with an estimating app for my weekend jobs, since I already use a chatbot now and then. I'd keep working for the firm and put more aside each month, maybe double what I do now. If a supervisor job came up, I'd go for it before the software makes it smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for my hands, for my ladder up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estimators, and Carol, the buyer who orders all our materials. She's been there twenty years and knows every supplier by name. If software does all the ordering, I don't know where a buyer with twenty years at the firm goes at 55.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your hands are fine. Your firm does big commercial jobs. Would robots touch those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this picture, slowly. The first robots would go where it's big, open and repetitive, like running lights across a warehouse ceiling. Old shops with odd ceilings and half the drawings wrong, that's people for a long time.

say: I'd say it's mostly the **office side's** problem.
I'd say the **trades** are the last thing to go.
think: The firm already **prices jobs** with software and didn't replace an estimator.

do: Learn an **estimating app** properly for weekend quotes.
**Double** the amount he saves each month.
Apply for the next **supervisor job** before software shrinks the role.
feel: **Uneasy** about his chance to move up, not about his hands-on work.
S1.quote: If software does all the ordering, I don't know where a buyer with twenty years at the firm goes at 55.
fieldNote: He has **seen it already**: an estimator left and software filled the gap.
His worry is the **career ladder**, not his current tools-on job.
He thinks robots start on **big, repetitive** sites and leave messy old buildings to people.

steps.text: Learn an estimating app properly for his weekend charger quotes
Keep working at Castleton and apply for the next supervisor job
Double the amount he puts into savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and that nobody voted for it. At the mosque on Friday, men my dad's age would talk about nothing else. I'd say keep your faith and keep working, because what else do you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think commercial fit-out is where the robots land first in 2031, because the sites are big and the drawings are already on computers. My firm's office side would go in 2028, and the bosses would be pricing robot crews by 2030. I'd be 32, probably married, and the work I know best would be first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the inspection and testing course within the first year; it's evenings for a few months and costs about a month's rent. I'd grow the weekend charger work into something with its own name, because people's houses will need someone they trust. And I'd save every bit of the weekend money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. But I'm a steady sort, I'd rather do something than sit and stew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned you'd likely be married by then. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, that's not up for debate with either family. But maybe a smaller wedding, and we'd put off buying a flat until we knew what my work looked like after 2031. Leah's job at the dental surgery is hands-on too, so neither of us is a desk worker, which helps a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say robots land on commercial work first. Why would homes last longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every house is different, and people don't want a machine wandering round their kid's bedroom. A shopping centre doesn't care who fits the lights, only the price. So my plan is to be the person a family calls, not the person a contractor hires by the hour.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and nobody voted for it.
I'd tell older men at the mosque to **keep working** and keep their faith.
think: Commercial fit-out is where robots land **first**, around **2031**.
The firm's **office side** goes in 2028, with robot crews priced by 2030.
At 32 he'd see the **work he knows best** go first.
do: Take the evening **inspection and testing** course within the first year.
Grow weekend charger work into a **named business** for households.
Hold a **smaller wedding** and delay buying a flat.
feel: **Worried**, but he'd rather act than sit and stew.
S2.quote: A shopping centre doesn't care who fits the lights, only the price.
fieldNote: He reads the **three-year gap** as time to move from commercial to home work.
He sees **homes as safer** because families want a trusted person, not a machine.
Both incomes are **hands-on**, which he counts as a small comfort.
He stays **in control**: a course, a side business and a smaller wedding.

steps.text: Take the evening inspection and testing course within a year
Build the weekend EV charger work into a named small business
Save every bit of the weekend job money
Hold a smaller wedding and delay buying a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd tell the apprentices on site to pick their side of the trade carefully, homes over big commercial jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2034 still hit my side of the work, just later. I'd be 35, which is late to start fresh but not too late if I've already moved over. The way I see it, the warning only helps if I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the testing qualification in the first year, like I said, then move from Castleton to a small domestic firm around 2029 to learn the house side properly. Meanwhile I'd save for a van and kit, about six months of money, so I could go on my own by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind of worry that gets me out of bed early, not the kind that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving a big firm means giving something up. What?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The steady pay, the pension the firm puts in, and Ray, who's been good to me. Small domestic firms pay a bit less to start. I'd have to tell Leah we tighten up for a year or two while I switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've called yourself someone who waits for proof. Isn't moving in 2029 a leap before the proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is a bit, and you're right to say it. But by 2029 I'd have watched the thinking AI hit our office, and that's my proof the next part is coming. I don't need to see the robot on my ladder to believe it's coming for the ladder.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if you start now.
I'd tell apprentices to choose **home work** over big commercial jobs.
think: Robots by **2034** still hit his side of the trade, just later.
At 35 it's late but **not too late**, if he has already moved over.
do: Pass the **testing qualification** in the first year.
Move to a small **domestic firm** around 2029 to learn house work.
Save **six months** of money for his own van and kit.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way that pushes him to act early.
S3.quote: I don't need to see the robot on my ladder to believe it's coming for the ladder.
fieldNote: He resolves the **proof versus leap** tension: AI in the office is his proof.
He accepts a **pay cut** and losing the firm's pension to make the switch.
His plan has **clear dates**: course now, new firm 2029, own business 2031.

steps.text: Pass the inspection and testing qualification in the first year
Move from Castleton to a small domestic firm around 2029
Save six months of money for his own van and kit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a fair run-up, and anyone young in a trade has time to sort themselves out. I'd tell my cousin's boy, who's starting college, to do electrics anyway, but the house side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three is 2039, and I'm 40 then. By then I'd hope to have my own small firm with a couple of lads, doing testing and house work, and maybe running whatever machines come. I don't think the job vanishes, I think it changes who holds the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Castleton a couple more years and try for supervisor, since there's no rush. I'd do the testing qualification by 2028 and start my own firm around 2030, buying a van on a small loan. I'd keep using the AI tools for quotes now and then, nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, a little uneasy. It's far enough off to plan for, close enough not to forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you're running machines in your own firm, are you the one doing the replacing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, and I've thought about that. If a robot can run the cable and I can sign it off and deal with the customer, I'd buy one the way my dad bought his first van. But I'd keep lads on as well, because a firm is people, and apprentices need somewhere to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin's boy, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the trade properly, every bit of it, testing included. Don't just learn to pull cable, because pulling cable is the bit a machine learns first. Learn to find faults and talk to people, that lasts.

say: I'd call it a **fair run-up** for anyone young in a trade.
I'd tell my cousin's boy to do **electrics anyway**, on the house side.
think: By **2039** he's 40 and hopes to run his own small firm.
The job doesn't vanish; it changes **who holds the tools**.
do: Stay at Castleton and try for **supervisor** for a couple of years.
Start his **own firm** around 2030 with a van on a small loan.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with a little unease that keeps him planning.
S4.quote: Don't just learn to pull cable, because pulling cable is the bit a machine learns first.
fieldNote: With a decade he **slows down**: supervisor first, own firm later.
He would **buy a robot** himself, like his dad's first van, but keep apprentices on.
His advice centres on **fault-finding and people**, the parts he thinks last.

steps.text: Stay at Castleton two more years and apply for supervisor
Get the inspection and testing qualification by 2028
Buy a van on a small loan and start his own firm around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Commercial work goes first and I'd have barely three years to get out of it. What would help is a leg up, not benefits: cheaper evening courses for testing and inspection, and small loans for trades people setting up on their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about apprentices. If firms stop taking them on because of all this, there'll be nobody left in fifteen years who knows how to check whether the robots did it right. Someone has to keep training young people, even if it costs the firms a bit.

headlineQuote: My plan is to be the person a family calls, not the person a contractor hires by the hour.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old electrician** at a forty-strong commercial fit-out firm, often on night shifts.
He rents with his fiancée **Leah** and earns extra fitting **EV chargers** on weekends.
He trusts things **once proven** and uses a chatbot lightly, always checking the book.
He's calm if AI stalls, but expects **commercial work** to meet robots first.
His answer to faster change is a **testing qualification** and a move to home work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because commercial work goes first and he'd have barely three years.
whatWouldHelp: Cheaper **evening courses** in testing and inspection.
**Small loans** for trades people setting up on their own.
